register: wave-6 authoring register (S-B6 tranche) — part 2 of 2

items.stem: Which extraction route is forced upon metals that sit above carbon in the reactivity series?
items.modelAnswer: They must be extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds — carbon is not a strong enough reducing agent for them.

items.stem: State the cheap reduction route used for metals below carbon, naming the reducing substance.
items.modelAnswer: Heating with carbon: the carbon reduces the metal out of its oxide, and carbon is a cheap reducing agent.

items.stem: Explain why the blast furnace needs no external heating once it is up and running.
items.modelAnswer: In the first zone the coke burns in the hot air, and that burning is exothermic — it gives out heat, which keeps the furnace at its working temperature, so the reaction effectively heats itself.

items.stem: Zinc sits just above iron in the reactivity series, and both oxides can be reduced by carbon monoxide in a furnace. Using the position-reactivity link, decide which of the two metals is harder to reduce from its oxide, and say why.
items.modelAnswer: Zinc is the harder of the two to reduce: it sits higher in the reactivity series, so it is more readily oxidised, and reduction is the reverse of the oxidation the metal readily undergoes — its oxide holds the oxygen more strongly.

items.stem: Starting from the ore, name the two preparation stages that ready aluminium oxide for the electrolysis cell.
items.modelAnswer: Bauxite is first purified to aluminium oxide, and the aluminium oxide is then dissolved in molten cryolite.

items.stem: State what happens at the cathode during aluminium extraction and where the product collects.
items.modelAnswer: Aluminium ions gain electrons at the cathode (Al3+ + 3e- -> Al), and the molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.

items.stem: Explain why dissolving the aluminium oxide in cryolite saves the plant money.
items.modelAnswer: Cryolite lowers the melting point of the mixture, so the electrolyte need not be heated to the very high melting point of pure aluminium oxide — the big energy cost of melting pure Al2O3 is avoided.

items.stem: A plant engineer finds the graphite anodes must be replaced every few weeks. Explain what is consuming them, naming the two reactants involved.
items.modelAnswer: The oxygen released at the anode (from oxide ions losing electrons) reacts with the hot graphite carbon, burning the anode away as carbon dioxide — oxygen plus carbon — so the anodes wear and need regular replacement.

items.stem: Name the three ions whose salts are soluble without exception, and the anion family that never forms an insoluble salt.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts all dissolve, and every nitrate is soluble — no nitrate is insoluble.

items.stem: State the default solubility of carbonates and of hydroxides in water.
items.modelAnswer: Most carbonates are insoluble and most hydroxides are insoluble — only the sodium, potassium and ammonium members dissolve (with calcium hydroxide only slightly soluble).

items.stem: Explain why a chemist cannot simply assume that all salts dissolve when planning how to prepare one.
items.modelAnswer: Because solubility decides the most appropriate preparation method: the rules say most members are soluble but carry firm exceptions (silver and lead(II) chlorides, barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates), and an insoluble salt must be prepared by a different route from a soluble one.

items.stem: A student plans to make lead(II) chloride and wonders whether it will dissolve once made. Predict its behaviour in water, citing the rule and the exception you used.
items.modelAnswer: It will not dissolve: common chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead(II), and lead(II) is one of the two named exceptions, so PbCl2 is an insoluble chloride.

items.stem: Which two chlorides refuse to dissolve no matter how much water is added?
items.modelAnswer: Silver chloride and lead(II) chloride — the two insoluble chloride exceptions.

items.stem: Give the chemical name and formula of limewater, and the gas it is used to test for.
items.modelAnswer: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)2, and it is the test for carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why a spoonful of sodium carbonate and a spoonful of calcium carbonate behave differently when each is shaken with water.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium is one of the three soluble carbonate members (sodium, potassium and ammonium), so sodium carbonate dissolves to a clear solution; calcium is not one of those members, and carbonates are otherwise insoluble, so calcium carbonate stays as a solid suspension.

items.stem: Three sulfates sit on the shelf: magnesium sulfate, barium sulfate and sodium sulfate. Two dissolve in water to give clear solutions and one stays solid. Identify the insoluble one and cite the rule.
items.modelAnswer: Barium sulfate stays solid: common sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead(II), and barium is on the insoluble list.

items.stem: What property of a solution does a titration analyse?
items.modelAnswer: Its concentration — a titration is a method of analysing the concentration of solutions.

items.stem: Name the three centre-piece pieces of apparatus in a titration setup.
items.modelAnswer: A burette, a pipette and a conical flask.

items.stem: Explain why a titration can prepare a salt as cleanly as it measures neutralisation.
items.modelAnswer: Because a titration finds exactly how much alkali neutralises a quantity of acid; repeating that neutralisation at the measured, controlled volumes lets the salt be prepared with no leftover acid or alkali.

items.stem: A titration finds the volume of hydrochloric acid that neutralises a measured alkali sample. State the three quantities this kind of result is used to calculate in exam questions.
items.modelAnswer: The moles present, the concentration of one of the solutions, or the volume needed for neutralisation — moles, concentration and volume are the three calculation targets.

items.stem: What must be flushed out of the burette's jet space before the first reading is taken?
items.modelAnswer: Air bubbles — a little acid is run through first to clear the jet space between the tap and the tip.

items.stem: How finely must each burette reading be recorded?
items.modelAnswer: To the nearest 0.05 cm3, read at eye level.

items.stem: Explain why the acid is added one drop at a time only near the endpoint, even though larger portions were fine earlier in the titration.
items.modelAnswer: Because the colour change at the endpoint is sharp: a whole portion run in past the endpoint would overshoot and spoil the titre, so drop-by-drop addition stops the first permanent change from being missed.

items.stem: Titre 1 reads 14.90 cm3 and Titre 2 reads 15.00 cm3. State whether the two results may be averaged, and justify the decision with the concordance rule.
items.modelAnswer: Yes: they differ by only 0.10 cm3, which is within the 0.1 cm3 concordance window, so the two results are concordant and may be averaged.

items.stem: Define oxidation in terms of oxygen.
items.modelAnswer: Oxidation is any reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

items.stem: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon and loses its oxygen to the carbon. Name the change the zinc oxide has undergone.
items.modelAnswer: Reduction — the zinc oxide has lost oxygen.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction between zinc and copper(II) oxide cannot be labelled as only an oxidation or only a reduction.
items.modelAnswer: Because both happen at once: zinc gains the oxygen while copper(II) oxide loses it, so oxidation and reduction occur together — the paired change is what earns the overall reaction the name redox.

items.stem: In the reaction Zn + CuO -> ZnO + Cu, identify the oxidising agent and justify the pick by following the oxygen's journey.
items.modelAnswer: Copper(II) oxide is the oxidising agent: it supplies the oxygen that the zinc takes up, so the CuO oxidises the zinc while it is itself reduced to copper.

items.stem: State the electron-transfer definitions of oxidation and reduction.
items.modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons — OIL RIG.

items.stem: What are spectator ions, and what happens to them when the ionic equation is written?
items.modelAnswer: Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides of the equation, so they are omitted from the ionic equation.

items.stem: Explain what splitting the ionic equation Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu into two half equations reveals that the single full equation hides.
items.modelAnswer: The half equations show the two electron movements separately — magnesium losing two electrons (oxidation) and Cu2+ gaining two electrons (reduction) — so the single line hides who gives the electrons and who receives them.

items.stem: Iron filings dropped into copper(II) sulfate solution become coated with brown copper as the blue colour fades. Describe what has happened to the Cu2+ ions in electron terms and name the change.
items.modelAnswer: The Cu2+ ions have gained electrons (the iron loses them, forming Fe2+), so the copper(II) ions are reduced to copper metal — that gain of electrons is reduction.

items.stem: State the two aluminium properties that suit aircraft bodies.
items.modelAnswer: Low density and high strength.

items.stem: Which metal is the standard choice for electrical wiring, and which two properties earn it that place?
items.modelAnswer: Copper: its electrical conductivity and its ductility make it the standard wiring metal.

items.stem: A can of tomatoes sits on the shelf for months, and the fruit inside is acidic. Explain why the aluminium can survives the acidic food.
items.modelAnswer: Aluminium is unreactive and shrugs off acidic foodstuffs, so the can metal does not react with the acid even over long storage.

items.stem: A new overhead cable run is to be strung across a valley and aluminium is chosen for it. Name the property behind the choice and state what the cable is carrying.
items.modelAnswer: Aluminium conducts electricity very well, and the cable carries an electric current along the overhead line.

items.stem: Which steel type suits car body panels, and what carbon content gives it that character?
items.modelAnswer: Mild steel: its low carbon content of about 0.25% leaves it soft and malleable enough to be pressed into panels.

items.stem: State the two metals alloyed into stainless steel and the property mix that justifies its use.
items.modelAnswer: Stainless steel mixes in about 20% chromium and 10% nickel, giving strength together with corrosion resistance.

items.stem: Mild steel, high-carbon steel and stainless steel behave very differently in the workshop. Explain what single variable produces those differences.
items.modelAnswer: The carbon content decides the character of the steel — the higher the carbon, the harder the steel — so mild steel (about 0.25% carbon) is soft and workable while high-carbon steel (0.5-1.4% carbon) is hard enough for tools.

items.stem: A joiner needs a chisel that keeps its cutting edge, and a coachbuilder needs panels that press into shape without cracking. Assign each job its steel type, justifying each with one property word.
items.modelAnswer: The chisel takes high-carbon steel — hard is the property that keeps a cutting edge (0.5-1.4% carbon); the coachbuilder takes mild steel — soft and malleable panels press without cracking (about 0.25% carbon).

items.stem: What makes a rock qualify as an ore of a metal?
items.modelAnswer: The rock must contain enough of the metal to make extracting it worthwhile.

items.stem: Name the three methods by which a metal can be won from its ore.
items.modelAnswer: Electrolysis, the blast furnace, or reaction with a more reactive material.

items.stem: Explain why extracting iron from haematite counts as a reduction of the ore.
items.modelAnswer: Haematite is an oxide ore — iron chemically joined to oxygen. Extraction removes that oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, and removing oxygen from a substance is exactly what reduction means.

items.stem: A prospector finds (a) a vein of metallic gold and (b) a rock rich in a copper compound. State which find needs no chemical extraction and why, using the two ways metals occur in the crust.
items.modelAnswer: The gold needs none: it is one of the native metals, found as the element itself in the crust, so there is no compound to break down — the copper, locked inside a compound in its rock, must be extracted chemically.

items.stem: Name the two metals given as examples that are mined straight out of the ground as elements.
items.modelAnswer: Gold and platinum are mined directly as the uncombined metals.

items.stem: Compared with ores such as haematite or bauxite, what processing stage do gold and platinum skip entirely?
items.modelAnswer: They skip all chemical extraction: the metals hardly react, so no processing is needed to separate them out of a compound.

items.stem: Use the idea of chemical stability to account for unreactive metals occurring free in nature.
items.modelAnswer: Their chemical stability stops them reacting with the other substances around them, so over time they remain the free element instead of joining into compounds.

items.stem: Pieces of metal X are stirred into a solution containing a compound of metal N: nothing happens. The test is repeated with metal M, and this time N deposits out of the solution. Rank M, N and X in reactivity, citing the rule you used.
items.modelAnswer: The rule: a metal can reduce another metal's compound only if it is the more reactive of the two. X displaced nothing, so X is less reactive than N; M displaced N, so M is more reactive than N. The order is M > N > X.
